newsitem.title: HAITI: Haiti pushes ahead with privatization plan.
newsitem.headline: Haiti pushes ahead with privatization plan.

text.p: After years of false starts and political turmoil, Haiti's parliament has approved a plan to allow private investment in public enterprises and to reassure the international community of its commitment to economic reform.
Hundreds of millions of dollars in foreign aid and loans to the impoverished country are conditioned on the Haitian government's commitment to privatization.

While the legislation adopted last week is a step towards showing the will to privatize, World Bank officials said they would await more concrete action, such as the actual privatization of a state company, before funding is released.
"We expect to see positive steps," said Wendeline DeZan, an operations analyst at World Bank. "Because the government has been so slow, we expect to see some proof and actions."
DeZan pointed to numerous false starts on the part of the Haitian government in its moves to privatize.
The administration of former president Jean-Bertrand Aristide had gotten as far as the bidding process before giving up, saying the incoming Rene Preval administration should take up the issue.
World Bank officials have been equally frustrated by the slow speed of getting privatization legislation approved.
"If they had signed onto this in the spring, the funding would have been released," said DeZan.
The aid from international donors is desperately needed by the Haitian government, which has a $125 million budget deficit for this year.

Although the Preval administration maintains $140 million in federal reserves, that money is not used to give the appearance of a healthy economy to potential investors. The country is run as a cash economy, in which debts must be met with incoming revenue.
At times that cash is not available, government workers are not paid.

A majority in the lower house of parliament approved the law on Thursday, ending debates and filibustering that dragged on for months. The law allows for concession agreements or joint ventures with investors who would manage, for instance, Haiti's electricity and telephone companies.
"We are very satisfied," said Deputy Alex Fils-Aime, who was frustrated by the slow process of the vote. "Now we have to watch the process by which the law is applied."
The amount to be released to Haiti pending World Bank approval is some $106 million, including monies from Switzerland, Germany, Canada and the European Community

All funding from the U.S. Agency for International Development and World Bank is slated to close the budget gap, while $25 million from the International Monetary Fund would go to Haiti's Central Bank to pay off dedbt.
A grant of $15 million from USAID is also conditioned on civil service reform in which the government is expected to lay off a high percetage of employees.
Ninety-three percent of Haiti's $136 million dollar budget goes to government operations and paychecks for what international economists consider a bloated workforce.
One of the largest donors is the European Community, which has conditioned $30 million on an improved trade structure to benefit agriculture.

In addition to skepticism about Haiti's will to privatize, highly placed World Bank officials are said to be deeply troubled by growing insecurity in Haiti, which could easily curtail investor interest.

In recent weeks, former soldiers of Haiti's disbanded military have threatened to "fill the streets with fire and blood" if their demands for back pay and the release of ex- soldiers from prison are not met.

The ex-soldiers are also widely believed to have carried out an attack last month on the Port-au-Prince police station and the Parliament building, which left a civilian dead and two police officers wounded.
The day after the attack, a leader and a member of a political party associated with the ex-military were assassinated.
